claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain and toughness relative to high-purity tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Ta, Ti, V, and Zr behave as dispersed solute atoms within a tungsten matrix in equimolar WTaTiVZr.
The dispersed refractory elements produce a solute-drag effect on moving dislocations.
Solute drag delays the formation of dislocation pile-ups.
Solute drag facilitates dynamic recovery.
Delayed pile-up formation and dynamic recovery produce smoother and more homogeneous plastic deformation.
High-purity tungsten exhibits comparatively abrupt failure under the proposed conditions.
Digital image correlation can measure local tensile-strain evolution and spatial strain distributions.
EBSD can be used to investigate deformation microstructures at regions having different local strain levels.
EBSD can specifically quantify the localization of dislocation-cell formation.
Grain-interior versus grain-boundary characterization can isolate intragranular solute drag from grain-boundary effects.
Testing at approximately 1000 °C in an inert atmosphere represents high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions.
WTaTiVZr will have a lower work-hardening rate than high-purity tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a delayed yield point relative to high-purity tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will accumulate strain more smoothly over larger plastic strains than high-purity tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will show less localized dislocation-cell formation than high-purity tungsten.
The predicted behavior is predominantly intragranular rather than controlled by grain-boundary phenomena.
The hypothesis is restricted to conditions where WTaTiVZr remains single-phase without secondary-phase precipitation or significant grain-boundary segregation.
Systematic changes in Ta, Ti, V, and Zr concentration should produce corresponding changes in work hardening, yield behavior, or strain homogeneity if solute drag is causal.
A lack of mechanical-response changes with altered solute concentration, or dominance of grain-boundary phenomena, would falsify the proposed solute-drag mechanism.
